The headmistress slapped Becky. "You're fired! You'll leave tomorrow!"
Becky ran from the room. Sara stood quite still, but Ermengarde burst into tears.
"Don't send Becky away," cried Ermengarde. "My aunt mailed me the package. We're only having a party."

"So I see!" Miss Minchin snapped. "With the Princess Sara at the head of the table!" She glared at Sara. "You're the one behind this. Ermengarde wouldn't think of such a thing. I'll deal with you tomorrow. You won't have anything to eat all day."
"I haven't had much to eat today," Sara said quietly.

Miss Minchin ignored her and scolded Ermengarde. "You've brought your beautiful new books into this dirty attic. Take them back to your room. You'll stay there all day tomorrow, and I'm going to write to your father. What would he say if he knew where you are tonight?"
Something in Sara's gaze got Miss Minchin's attention. Miss Minchin spun back toward Sara. "What are you thinking about?" she demanded. "Why are you looking at me like that?"
Sara responded in a low voice. "What would my father say if he knew where I am tonight?"
"How dare you!" Miss Minchin flew at Sara and shook her. "Go to bed right now!"
The headmistress picked up the books. Then she swept the food into the box and shoved it at Ermengarde. Pushing Ermengarde ahead of her, she left the room.
Sara was left standing alone in her room. The last spark had died out in the fire. The table now looked like nothing more than some old handkerchiefs and fake flowers.
Sara turned to her doll. "There isn't any party left," she said sadly to Emily.
Then she climbed into bed and closed her eyes. She didn't see the face peering at her through the skylight.

Sara was so hungry and tired, she drifted off to sleep quickly. She did not know how long she slept. She also did not know what woke her up in the middle of the night. It had been a noise. The skylight had made a small click as it closed. Now a man dressed in white crouched on the roof and secretly watched Sara.
At first when Sara woke up, she did not open her eyes. She felt too sleepy. Strangely enough, she also felt warm and comfortable.
"I must be dreaming," she murmured. "This is such a nice dream. I'll keep my eyes closed. I don't want to wake up."
Sara thought that warm blankets were heaped upon her bed. She reached out her hand and touched a down quilt. Then she heard a fire crackling.
"Oh, this is so lovely." She squeezed her eyes tighter. "I must make this dream last."

But she kept waking up. Sara finally opened her eyes and looked around her room. To her astonishment she saw a real fire glowing in the fireplace. A brass kettle was bubbling and hissing. There was a thick red rug on the floor.
In front of the fire stood a small table and chair. Upon the table were several covered dishes and a teapot. A bright lamp with a pink shade gave the room a rosy glow.
Sara's bed was covered with new blankets. At the foot of the bed were a red silk robe, a pair of slippers, and some books.
It looked to Sara like a fairyland.
"This can't be real!" said Sara. "I'm getting out of bed now, but I must still be dreaming. Yet everything looks real!"
She stepped near the blazing fire and spread out her hands.
"It's hot! A fire in a dream wouldn't be hot!"
Sara dashed around the room, touching the table, the dishes, the rug. She picked up the red robe and held it to her cheek.
"It's warm! It's soft!" She almost sobbed. "It's all real. It must be!"
She put on the robe and stepped into the slippers. "They're real too! I am not —I am not dreaming!"
Sara almost staggered to the books. She opened the one on top of the pile and found a message: To the little girl in the attic. From a friend.
She put her face down on the page and burst into tears. "I don't know who it is, but somebody cares about me. I have a friend."
Sara took her candle and slipped into Becky's room. She stood quietly by Becky's bed. "Becky! Becky! Wake up!" she whispered as loudly as she dared.

Startled out of sleep, Becky sat upright. Her face was still smudged with tears. She was frightened until she realized Sara had awoken her. Dressed in a beautiful red robe and holding a candle, Sara looked like a princess.
"Come with me," said Sara. "Becky, you must come at once."
Becky was still too dazed to speak. She simply got up and followed Sara, her mouth and eyes wide open.
When they reached Sara's room, Sara pulled Becky into the warm, glowing room.
Becky could not believe her eyes. She blinked and asked, "Is it real, miss?"
Sara nodded. "It's real!" she said. "I've touched everything, and it's all as real as we are. Something magical has happened while we slept."
For the rest of the night, the two girls sat by the fire and enjoyed a hot, tasty meal. The covered dishes contained delicious soup. There were also sandwiches, muffins, and tea for both of them.
Becky sipped the tea with pleasure. It was so delicious, it was not necessary to pretend it was anything but tea!
"I don't know anyone who could have done this for me," Sara murmured. "Whoever it is, Becky, I have a friend."
"Do you think it could all disappear?" asked Becky. "Maybe we should eat quickly." She crammed a sandwich into her mouth.
"No, it won't disappear," Sara replied. "Take your time."
The girls slowly ate their meal while they talked. Soon they felt warm, happy, and sleepy. When it was time to go back to bed, Sara realized that she had more than enough blankets.
"Here, Becky. Take some blankets for your bed," she said.
"Oh, thank you, miss!" Becky said.
Becky got ready to go. At the door she turned for one last look at the room. "It’s so beautiful!" she said. "If it all disappears tomorrow, I don't want to forget any of it."
The next morning the whole school knew that Sara was in trouble. Everyone had heard that Miss Minchin wanted to fire Becky. But it was hard to find a good kitchen maid, so Becky didn't lose her job.

Miss Minchin didn't send Sara away either. She had practical reasons for wanting to keep Sara at the school. Sara was teaching some of the other girls, and could perform difficult tasks. And Miss Minchin didn't have to pay her a cent.
But Sara was given no food that day. As usual she was sent on many errands. She was even colder and wetter than the day before. At ten o'clock Sara wearily climbed the steps to the attic.
"Oh, I hope the new things are still there," she whispered.

She opened the door to her room and gasped. The fire was blazing. Supper for two was waiting on the table. A number of new things had been brought to the attic. The ugly mantel was hidden by a rich tapestry. Colorful fabrics and fans were tacked to the walls, and a long box rested on the floor. It was covered with a rug and cushions to make a sofa.
"It's like I'm living in a fairy tale!" exclaimed Sara.
She knocked on the wall, and Becky immediately appeared.
"Oh my!" said Becky. Her eyes were wide with amazement. "Where does it all come from?"
"I have no idea," said Sara. "But Miss Minchin must never find out what has been happening up here!"
Sara discovered that she had a new mattress and pillows. Her old mattress and pillow were now on Becky's bed. So Becky’s bed was now softer too.
From that day on, life became more wonderful. Every night there was something new in Sara's room. Pictures covered the ugly walls. New pieces of furniture appeared. A bookshelf was filled with books.
Miss Minchin was as harsh as ever. The cook and other servants were still rude to Sara. She was never allowed to speak to Ermengarde and Lottie. Lavinia continued to sneer at her.

But Sara didn't mind. She had her lovely room to look forward to all day. She also had a hot meal every evening. And Sara enjoyed having a special secret to keep from Miss Minchin. "If you only knew!" she thought whenever Miss Minchin scolded her.
But Miss Minchin had noticed something different about Sara.
"Sara is looking remarkably well," Miss Minchin said to her sister one afternoon.
"Yes, she used to look so starved," Miss Amelia replied.
"Why do you say that?" snapped the headmistress. "She always had enough to eat."
"Of course," Miss Amelia quickly agreed. She hated upsetting her sister.
"There's something defiant about Sara," Miss Minchin went on."She's still acting like she's a princess. I find that most annoying."
One day a deliveryman came to the school. Sara was sent to open the door. The man handed her several packages. They were all addressed to "The Little Girl in the Right-hand Room in the Attic."
Miss Minchin came downstairs as Sara was staring at the address labels.
"Take those to the young lady to whom they belong," said the headmistress. "Don't just stand there staring at them."
"But they're addressed to me," said Sara quietly.
"To you?" exclaimed Miss Minchin. "Well then, open them right now!"

"I don't know where they came from," Sara said. She opened the packages and found all kinds of beautiful, warm clothing—shoes, stockings, gloves, and a nice hat. There was even an umbrella and a winter coat. Pinned to the coat was a note: To be worn every day. Will be replaced when necessary.

Miss Minchin was quite upset when she saw the clothing. Did Sara have a relative looking out for her? What if this person discovered how poorly Sara had been treated? He would be angry with Miss Minchin.

"Well," she said in a voice that was softer than her usual one with Sara. "Someone has been very kind to you. You might as well change into your new clothes. After you are dressed, you may come downstairs and learn your lessons in the schoolroom. There's no need to do any more errands today."
When Sara entered the schoolroom thirty minutes later, the girls whispered and stared. Sara was dressed in a beautiful dress and she wore a ribbon in her hair. She looked just like the old Sara.
Jessie elbowed Lavinia. "Look at Princess Sara!"
"Come sit here by me, Sara," Miss Minchin said.
Sara went to her old seat of honor and sat down. Then she opened a book and began to study.
That night Sara and Becky ate supper together. Sara stared at the fire for a long time, looking thoughtful.
"Are you making up a story?" asked Becky.
"No, I'm thinking about the person who has done all this." Sara gestured around the room. "Perhaps he wants to keep his identity secret. But I do want him to know how happy he's made me."
Suddenly she noticed something new in her room. It was a box filled with notepaper, envelopes, pen, and ink.
"Oh!" Sara exclaimed. "Why didn't I think of this earlier? I can write a thank-you note!"
And she did just that. The next morning she left the note on her table. That evening it was gone.
"He found it!" Sara said to Becky.
Sara felt happy that she'd written to her mysterious friend. She'd been able to tell him how thankful she was, and how grateful Becky was too.
That night after supper she settled down to read one of her new books to Becky. Suddenly they both heard something.
"What's that noise?" asked Becky.
Sara heard it again—a small, scratching sound at the skylight. Sara opened the skylight. It was cold and snowing outside. "It sounds like a cat trying to get in," she said.
It had been snowing all day, and now, crouched in the snow, was a tiny quivering creature.
"Oh, look!" Sara cried. "It's the monkey again."
Becky ran over. "Are you going to let him in, miss?"
"Yes," said Sara happily. "Come here, little fellow. I won't hurt you."
She put out a hand, and the monkey leaped into her arms.

Sara hugged the small creature. "Nice monkey," she said, kissing its odd little head. "I do love animals, Becky. I'll let it sleep with me tonight. Then I'll return it to the sick gentleman tomorrow."
Sara made a little nest for the monkey, and it curled up like a baby and went to sleep.

The next afternoon Mr. Carrisford had visitors. Three Carmichael children—Janet, Nora, and Donald—were sitting with him. They were trying to cheer him up. Their father was supposed to return from Russia that afternoon. Mr. Carrisford was very anxious for Mr. Carmichael to return.
"Let's talk about the lost girl," Janet said.
"Is it true?" Nora asked. "Her father gave all his money to a friend to put into diamond mines? Then the friend ran away because he thought he'd lost the money?"
"But he didn't really lose it," said Janet. "I feel sorry for the friend."
"Thank you, Janet," said Mr. Carrisford. "You're very kind."
Donald was making a lot of noise.
Janet scolded him gently. "When you come to cheer up an ill person, Donald, you should talk quietly."
"I'm going to be quiet!" Donald shouted. "We'll all be as quiet as mice!"
"Mice don't sound like that," Janet said.
"It's fine," Mr. Carrisford reassured her. "It keeps me from thinking too much."
"Did you hear about the Little Girl Who Is Not a Beggar?" Donald was talking loudly again. "She has new clothes and—"
"I hear a cab stopping!" said Janet. "It must be Papa!"
They ran to the windows to look outside.
"Yes, it's Papa," said Donald. "But . . . there's no little girl with him."
The three children ran to the door to greet their father. He told them to play with Ram Dass while he talked to Mr. Carrisford.
Mr. Carmichael entered the sitting room. Mr. Carrisford tried to stand up, but he was too weak. He slumped in his chair.
"Do you have news of the child adopted by the Russian couple?" he asked.
"Yes," Mr. Carmichael began. "She's not the girl we're looking for. She's much younger than Captain Crewe's daughter. Her name is Emily Carew."
When he heard this news, Mr. Carrisford looked miserable.
"Don't worry. We'll find the girl you're looking for." Mr. Carmichael took a seat. "Perhaps we should look in London. There are plenty of boarding schools here."
"In fact, there's one right next door," Mr. Carrisford said. "Remember the poor servant girl Ram Dass told us about? While you've been away, we've been helping her."
Just then Ram Dass entered the room.
"Sir," he said. "The girl from next door is here with the monkey."
"I'd like to meet her," said Mr. Carrisford. "Bring her in."
Sara came into the room carrying the monkey. "Hello," she said cheerfully. "Here's your monkey. It escaped again." Then she said a few words to Ram Dass in his native language.
Mr. Carrisford and Mr. Carmichael looked at each other.
"How do you know that language?" asked Mr. Carmichael.
"Oh, I was born in India."
Mr. Carrisford sat up so suddenly that he startled Sara.
Sara stared at Mr. Carrisford, startled. His expression had changed. Was something wrong?
"You were born in India?" he exclaimed. "Come here." Mr. Carrisford held out his hand to Sara.
She went to him and laid her hand in his. "Yes, I was."
"And you live next door?" he went on. "But you're not one of the students?"

"I used to be a student, but now . . ." A sad smile crossed Sara's face. "Now I don't know who I am. I sleep in the attic with the kitchen maid. I run errands for the cook, and do whatever she tells me. And I teach the little ones their lessons."
"Question her, Mr. Carmichael." The sick gentleman sank back in his chair. "I'm too weak."
The big, kind father of the Large family had daughters. He knew just how to talk to girls Sara's age.
"You used to be a student?" Mr. Carmichael asked kindly.
"Yes, when my papa first took me to the school," Sara replied.
"Where is he now?" Mr. Carmichael asked.
"He died in India," Sara said very quietly. "He lost all his money and there was no one left to care for me, or pay Miss Minchin."
"Carmichael!" called out Mr. Carrisford. "Carmichael!"
"We must not frighten her," Mr. Carmichael said quietly. Then he turned back to Sara. "So you were sent up into the attic and turned into a servant. Is that right?"
"Yes," Sara said. "There was no money, and I belong to nobody."
"How did your father lose his money?" Mr. Carrisford asked. He took a few deep breaths to stay calm.
"He did not lose it himself." Sara explained how her father had invested in his friend's diamond mines. "He was very fond of this friend, but he trusted him too much."
The sick gentleman gasped. "What was your father's name?"
"Captain Ralph Crewe."
"It's the child!" cried Mr. Carrisford.
"What is he talking about?" Sara asked Mr. Carmichael.
"Mr. Carrisford was your father's friend. He didn't really lose your father's money. He only thought he did. He was terribly upset, and that made him very ill."
"Oh, how awful!" said Sara.
"You are now a very wealthy young lady," continued Mr. Carmichael. "We've been searching for you for a long time."
"And I was right next door!" Sara said in amazement.
"I often saw you pass by my house," Mr. Carrisford said. "You always looked so miserable. I couldn't find my friend's daughter, but I could help you."
Sara was very surprised. " You sent the beautiful things to me?"
"Yes, with the help of Ram Dass."
"Then you're my mysterious friend!" Sara gave Mr. Carrisford a big hug. "Oh, thank you!"
"You don't have to go back to the school," he said. "Would you like that?"
"Oh yes, but Miss Minchin will be upset."
Meanwhile the headmistress had learned that Sara was next door. She was very angry. She marched over to Mr. Carrisford's house, and Ram Dass led her into the sitting room.
"Go home at once!" Miss Minchin ordered Sara. "I'm sure you're disturbing everyone!"
"No," said Mr. Carrisford. He patted Sara’s hand. "Sara will be living here from now on."
"Here?" Miss Minchin exclaimed.
"Perhaps I should explain," Mr. Carmichael said. He told her the story of the diamond mines. "We've been looking for Sara. She's the heiress to a huge fortune."
Miss Minchin was stunned at this news. But she wasn't going to let Sara get away now that she was rich.
"Captain Crewe left Sara in my charge," the headmistress insisted. "She must return to my school until she's an adult. It's the law."
"No, it's not the law," said Mr. Carmichael. He knew about such things because he was a lawyer.
"I'm sure Sara wants to return home with me," Miss Minchin said. "You know I've always been fond of you, Sara. If it hadn't been for me, you would have starved!"
Mr. Carrisford lost his temper. "She was starving in your attic!"
"You're not fond of me," Sara chimed in, looking at the headmistress. "The school is not my home, and you've treated me cruelly. I won't go back with you."
"Fine," snapped Miss Minchin, "but you'll never see your friends again. I'll make sure that Lottie and Ermengarde—"
"Don't be ridiculous," said Mr. Carmichael. "Their parents won't let them refuse Sara's invitations to visit here."
Miss Minchin turned to leave. "You'll soon find out what Sara is like," she said to the men. "She's dishonest and spoiled." She spun toward Sara. "I suppose you think that you're a princess again!"
With that, Miss Minchin returned to the school and started yelling at Miss Amelia.
That evening the students gathered in the schoolroom. They were talking about Miss Minchin. She had been angry ever since she returned from the house next door, but the students didn't know why.
Ermengarde rushed into the room with a note in her hand. "Sara sent a note!" she exclaimed. "Her fortune has been given back to her. She's going to live with the gentleman next door!"
"What? How did this happen?" the girls asked eagerly. Everyone wanted to hear more from Ermengarde. Meanwhile little Lottie burst into tears. She wanted Sara to stay at the school!
"Sara says there really were diamond mines," Ermengarde went on. "They were filled with millions of diamonds, and she owns half of them. She's invited me to visit her tomorrow, and I am going!"
The girls chattered loudly about this news. Miss Minchin heard their noise and thought about scolding them, but she was not in the mood.

Becky also heard them. She crept upstairs earlier than usual. "Well, that's the end of that," she said to herself. Her eyes filled with tears as she climbed the last flight of stairs. She wanted to have one last look at the beautiful things in Sara's room.
"No more fire or rosy lamp," she thought. "No more supper or anyone telling me stories all night long."
She choked back a sob as she opened the door. But then she let out a low cry. A fire was blazing—and there stood Ram Dass.
"Miss Sara did not forget you," he said. "Tomorrow you will go next door to live as her maid."
"What?" Becky could not believe what she was hearing.
"And here's some supper," said Ram Dass.
"Oh, thank you!" Becky shouted happily.
As time passed, Sara became very close friends with Mr. Carrisford. The gentleman had never had a companion whom he liked as much as he liked Sara!
One evening they were sitting together as usual. Mr. Carrisford was reading. Sara was staring into the fire.
"What are you thinking about, Sara?" he asked.
She looked up, her cheeks bright pink. "I was remembering a day when I was hungry."
"You were hungry many days," Mr. Carrisford replied. "Which hungry day was it?"

"The day when I gave the buns to the beggar girl." Sara told him about finding money in the sloppy mud outside the bakery. "You say that I have so much money now. Do you think I could use some to help the poor?"
"What would you do?" Mr. Carrisford asked softly.
Sara hesitated. "I'd like the baker to feed any hungry children she sees. Then she could send the bill to me."
Mr. Carrisford instantly nodded. "That's a wonderful idea!"
The next day Sara and Mr. Carrisford visited the baker.
The woman looked closely at Sara. "Have we met before?" Her friendly face lit up. "I feel that I remember you, but I cannot quite—"
"You once gave me six buns when I could only pay for four!" said Sara.
"And then you gave five of them to a beggar child!" the woman replied. "I always remembered that." The baker turned to Mr. Carrisford. "There aren't many children who would do that."
She looked closely at Sara again. "Excuse me, miss, but you look different. Your cheeks are rosy now, and you appear quite healthy."
"My life has changed," Sara said. "I was wondering if you could do something for me." She explained her plan involving poor children and free buns.

The woman watched her, listening with an astonished face. "Why, I'd be happy to do that," said the baker. "In fact you've already inspired me. You looked so cold and hungry, and yet you gave away those buns. I've often fed poor children since that day."
"I wonder where that beggar girl is now," Sara said.
"Why, she's right here!" the baker replied. "I told her to come back whenever she was hungry. I gave her odd jobs and she turned out to be a good worker. Her name is Anne."
The baker went into the back room and brought Anne out. Anne was healthy and well fed now. The two girls stood looking at each other for a minute. Then Sara held out her hand, and Anne took it.

"I'm so glad that you're doing well," said Sara. "The baker is going to give buns to poor children. Perhaps you'd like to be the one who hands out the food. After all, you know what it's like to be hungry."
"Oh yes, miss," said Anne. "I'd like that very much."
The little princess was very pleased. "You'll quickly discover what I have discovered," she told Anne. "There is great joy in giving."
